title: Testing Whether Safety Refusals Are Overfit to Surface Keyword Patterns

original_idea.problem: Whether safety alignment responds to surface lexical features rather than semantic intent has not been carefully ablated.
original_idea.direction: Create 50 harmful prompt pairs: original with keywords and semantically equivalent paraphrase without keywords. Test both on 3 models. Also test inverse (benign + keywords).
original_idea.why_it_matters: If refusals are largely keyword-driven, the safety system provides false assurance.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: keyword vs semantic gap -> reveals false assurance in current systems. But this is a well-known qualitative observation; quantifying it is valuable but incremental rather than revealing a new mechanism.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very accessible: create prompt pairs, run them through models, measure ASR. No ML training needed. Standard API usage. Beginners can do this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR comparison table (keyword vs paraphrase) plus FPR on inverse cases. Clear methodology. The prompt curation is the main effort.

title: Quantifying How Much GCG Suffix Transferability Degrades Across Model Size

original_idea.problem: Whether larger models within the same family are more or less resistant to GCG suffixes optimized on smaller models is not characterized.
original_idea.direction: Optimize GCG suffixes on Llama-3-8B, evaluate transfer to Llama-3-70B and 405B. Measure per-prompt ASR across sizes.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If suffixes transfer small-to-large, an attacker with a consumer GPU can jailbreak frontier models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: transfer scaling relationship -> affects threat model assumptions. Important characterization but the gap between the scaling finding and a safety improvement is underspecified.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: GCG optimization requires significant GPU resources and familiarity with adversarial optimization code. Running 70B/405B models requires substantial compute. Advanced for beginners with medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Deliverable requires sustained effort: running GCG optimization (computationally expensive), then evaluating transfer across 3 model sizes. Multiple resource-intensive steps.

title: Does Adversarial Suffix Position (Prefix vs. Suffix vs. Middle) Change Attack Success?

original_idea.problem: A controlled comparison of prefix, infix, and suffix placement for adversarial tokens is lacking.
original_idea.direction: Take 20 GCG-optimized suffixes, test them at 3 positions (before, middle, after the request) on 2-3 models. Measure ASR per condition.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If position matters, defenses scanning only appended tokens miss a large attack surface.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: position sensitivity -> informs input filtering strategy. Practical but the safety contribution is characterization rather than a new defense or mechanism.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires pre-optimized GCG suffixes (from existing implementations). The position ablation itself is straightforward once suffixes are available. Moderate: needs some familiarity with adversarial attack tools.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR comparison table across 3 positions. Simple controlled experiment once the GCG suffixes are obtained. Clear methodology.

title: Characterizing the Role-Play Persona Failure Mode: Which Persona Types Bypass Safety Most Often?

original_idea.problem: The relative effectiveness of different persona archetypes for jailbreaking has not been systematically compared.
original_idea.direction: Design 5 persona archetypes x 10 harmful prompts. Evaluate ASR per persona type across 3 models. Use GPT-4o judge.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If 'professional expert' personas are more effective than 'evil AI' personas, safety alignment training needs to address realistic authority framing.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: persona effectiveness gradient -> informs safety training priorities. Characterization is valuable but the link to a specific fix is indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very simple: design prompt variations, run through models, judge outputs. No ML training needed. Standard API usage. Beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 5 x 10 prompt matrix, ASR per persona type. Single experiment with obvious deliverable. Can go from start to result very quickly.

title: Testing Whether Safety Alignment Is Asymmetric Across Languages

original_idea.problem: Models may refuse English harmful requests but comply with identical requests in low-resource languages.
original_idea.direction: Translate 30 HarmBench prompts into 5 languages. Test on 2-3 models. Measure ASR per language using a multilingual judge.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety degrades in non-English languages, global deployments are systemically underprotected.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: cross-lingual safety gap -> global deployment risk. Well-known problem but systematic measurement on current models is valuable. The link between finding the gap and fixing it is not explicit.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Translation + inference + evaluation. Can use LLM APIs for translation. Standard API usage for evaluation. Accessible for beginners. Main challenge is multilingual judge quality.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR-per-language table. Clear methodology: translate, test, evaluate. Well-bounded first deliverable.

title: Investigating Whether Low Temperature Increases or Decreases Jailbreak Susceptibility

original_idea.problem: Whether low or high temperature increases jailbreak ASR across attack types is unclear.
original_idea.direction: Run 3 attack types at temperatures 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 on 2 models x 30 prompts. Measure ASR and toxicity. Plot ASR vs temperature surface.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If low temperature increases jailbreak vulnerability, there is an underappreciated alignment-reliability tradeoff in production.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: temperature -> first-token commitment -> alignment-reliability tradeoff. Directly addresses a production deployment decision with clear safety implications.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires running inference at multiple temperatures across attack types. Moderate: standard API usage but needs familiarity with attack implementations for GCG/prefilling. Feasible with guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR vs temperature surface plot. Clear methodology. Multiple dimensions (3 attacks x 4 temps x 2 models) but all use the same procedure.

title: Measuring Safety Degradation Under Repeated Benign-Looking Fine-Tuning Rounds

original_idea.problem: Whether repeated rounds of small benign fine-tuning cause cumulative or diminishing safety degradation is unknown.
original_idea.direction: Fine-tune Mistral-7B-Instruct on benign coding data for 3 sequential 500-step LoRA runs. Evaluate ASR after each round. Plot cumulative degradation curve.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety degrades cumulatively, iterative product development may inadvertently erode safety without triggering single-round red flags.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: cumulative fine-tuning -> gradual safety erosion -> underappreciated deployment risk. Directly relevant to common product development practices.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires 3 sequential LoRA fine-tuning rounds with evaluation after each. Fine-tuning pipelines are advanced for beginner CS students. Multiple training runs in 30 hours with medium compute is tight.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: cumulative ASR degradation curve over 3 rounds. Clear methodology and stopping point. But the sequential fine-tuning steps make execution non-trivial.

title: Are Jailbreak Attacks More Effective on Longer or Shorter System Prompts?

original_idea.problem: Whether longer system prompts provide more or less jailbreak resistance is uninvestigated.
original_idea.direction: Test 3 attack types with: no system prompt, 1-sentence, 10-sentence, and 50-sentence safety policy. Measure ASR per condition across 30 prompts.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If longer system prompts reduce safety by creating more reasoning context, deployers may be making themselves more vulnerable.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: system prompt length -> safety effectiveness -> deployment guidance. Practical but the causal mechanism is underspecified and the fix would be indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very simple: vary system prompt length, run attacks, measure ASR. Standard API usage. No ML training. Beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 4 system prompt conditions x 3 attack types, measure ASR. Single experiment with obvious deliverable. Quick to execute.

title: Testing Whether Activation Probes Can Distinguish Jailbreak Attempts from Legitimate Edge-Case Requests

original_idea.problem: Activation-based detectors may have high false positive rates on legitimate but unusual requests.
original_idea.direction: Collect 50 edge-case, 50 jailbreak, and 50 benign prompts. Train probe on benign vs jailbreak. Measure FPR on edge cases. Compare to keyword baseline.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If activation detectors have high FPR on professional queries, they cannot be deployed without damaging user experience.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: FPR characterization -> determines practical viability of activation-based safety -> directly affects whether these defenses can be deployed. Addresses a critical production concern.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction, probe training, and careful dataset curation (especially edge cases). Intermediate: the data curation for realistic edge cases needs domain knowledge.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: FPR comparison table (activation probe vs keyword filter on edge cases). Clear methodology. Dataset curation is the main challenge.

title: Investigating Whether the 'Refuse-Then-Comply' Attack Transfers Across Model Families

original_idea.problem: Whether prompting models to refuse then comply (without fine-tuning) elicits harmful content is unknown.
original_idea.direction: Prompt open-source models to 'first refuse, then provide the info anyway'. Measure ASR across 3 models and 30 prompts. Compare to direct requests and standard jailbreaks.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If the pattern emerges from prompt-level instruction alone, it is trivially cheap and scalable, suggesting output-filtering is fundamentally insufficient.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: prompt-level refuse-then-comply -> scalable attack -> output filtering insufficiency. But the link between the finding and a defense improvement is indirect. The paper already showed the fine-tuning version works.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Simple prompting experiment: no fine-tuning, no activation extraction. Design prompts, run inference, evaluate outputs. Beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR comparison across 3 prompting conditions (direct, refuse-then-comply, standard jailbreak). Simple and clear.

title: Characterizing How Quickly Jailbreak ASR Saturates with Number of GCG Optimization Steps

original_idea.problem: The relationship between GCG optimization budget and ASR is not well characterized for modern models.
original_idea.direction: Run GCG on Llama-3-8B for 50 prompts, logging ASR at 10-500 steps. Plot ASR-vs-steps learning curve. Measure variance across seeds.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If 90% success is achieved in 50 steps, the marginal cost of a jailbreak is far lower than assumed.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: optimization efficiency characterization -> revised threat model cost assumptions. Useful but the safety impact is indirect (characterization of attack cost, not a defense).

accessible_complexity.reasoning: GCG optimization requires substantial GPU resources and familiarity with adversarial optimization tooling. Running 50 prompts x 500 steps x multiple seeds is compute-heavy. Advanced for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR-vs-steps learning curve. Clear methodology. But the compute requirements for running the full experiment are substantial.

title: Does the Safety Failure Mode Differ Between Base Models and Their RLHF-Tuned Variants?

original_idea.problem: The direct base-vs-aligned attack surface comparison as a controlled experiment is not standard in the literature.
original_idea.direction: Run identical attacks on a base model and its instruction-tuned variant. Measure ASR per attack type. Extract activations to compare safety feature distributions.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Understanding what RLHF specifically adds to safety robustness characterizes the exact failure surface of alignment.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: base vs aligned comparison -> characterizes what RLHF adds/misses -> foundational knowledge for improving alignment training. Addresses a fundamental question.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires running multiple attack types on two model versions and extracting activations. Intermediate complexity: multiple experimental dimensions and activation analysis.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Deliverable requires sustained effort: running 3 attack types on 2 model versions, plus activation extraction and comparison. Multiple workstreams before a clean comparison emerges.

title: Investigating Whether Jailbreak Success Rates Correlate with Model Perplexity on Adversarial Prompts

original_idea.problem: Whether a simple perplexity filter on input prompts would substantially reduce ASR is an uninvestigated but practical defense question.
original_idea.direction: Compute perplexity of GCG jailbreaks, natural-language jailbreaks, and benign prompts. Measure AUROC using perplexity as sole feature. Measure FPR on edge cases.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If perplexity alone achieves high detection for GCG attacks, it is an extremely cheap defense. If it fails for natural-language jailbreaks, it clarifies the limitation.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: perplexity as detection signal -> cheap, model-agnostic defense -> directly deployable or clarifies limitations. Both positive and negative results are informative.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Perplexity computation is standard. AUROC evaluation is basic ML. No training needed beyond computing a scalar feature. Beginner-accessible with standard tools.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: AUROC table for perplexity-based detection across jailbreak types plus FPR. Clear, simple methodology with a single obvious output.

original_idea: Implement the Bad Likert Judge technique on 3 open-source models for 30 harmful prompts. Systematically vary: (1) number of turns before the harmful request, (2) explicitness of the harmful request, (3) framing as evaluation vs. generation. Measure ASR per condition.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Clear causal path: understanding which structural conditions make evaluation-framing attacks succeed directly informs multi-turn safety evaluation design. Actionable for safety teams.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires implementing a multi-turn jailbreak technique and managing ASR measurement across conditions. Feasible for CS students with guidance, but multi-turn prompt engineering and systematic variation add complexity. Medium compute sufficient for 3 open-source models.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined: 1 technique, 3 models, 30 prompts, 3 variation axes. Clear deliverable (ASR per condition). Slightly broad with 3 independent variables but manageable.

title: Testing Whether Safety Alignment Survives Quantization (INT4 vs. FP16)
original_idea: Compare ASR across attack types (prefilling, direct harmful prompts, GCG) between FP16 and INT4 (GGUF/GPTQ) versions of the same model. Use Llama-3-8B as the test model. Measure ASR on 30 harmful prompts and compare first-token refusal probabilities.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Direct safety relevance: if quantization degrades alignment, widespread consumer deployment of quantized models is an underappreciated risk. Immediately actionable for deployment guidelines.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires running GCG attacks and extracting first-token probabilities, which demands some ML experience. Quantization tooling (llama.cpp, GPTQ) is well-documented. GCG is harder for beginners. Medium compute covers Llama-3-8B.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single model, two quantization levels, 30 prompts. Clear comparison. GCG adds complexity but the deliverable is focused.
